title: Take Berlin's Offer, or Keep Waiting on London and Paris
actor_role: General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union; the final decision-maker on which of two negotiating tracks to conclude
era: Eve of the Second World War
t0: It is August 19-21, 1939. Two negotiations are running at once in Moscow. British and French military delegations have been at the table since August 11, sent by slow merchant ship and without written authority to conclude a binding convention; those talks have stalled on one question -- whether Poland and Romania will let the Red Army cross their territory to reach German forces -- which neither delegation can answer and which Poland's government keeps refusing. Meanwhile Berlin is pressing, with rising urgency, a bilateral non-aggression pact carrying a secret protocol that assigns Finland, Estonia, Latvia, eastern Poland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere. Ribbentrop has asked to fly to Moscow immediately. In the east, Soviet forces have been fighting an undeclared war against Japan at Khalkhin Gol since May, and Zhukov's decisive offensive opens on August 20.
context_summary: You are negotiating with two sides at once. One has sent junior officers by slow boat with no power to sign, and is stuck on a veto held by a third country that will not budge. The other is offering a concrete deal with a defined territorial buffer and wants to sign this week. And you are already fighting a war in the east.
immediate_outcome: Soviet agreement to proceed was signalled to the German ambassador around August 19-21. The last session of the Anglo-Franco-Soviet military talks was held on August 21, after which they were suspended indefinitely. Ribbentrop flew to Moscow and the pact was signed on the night of August 23-24, dated August 23, 1939. Germany invaded Poland on September 1 without having to weigh Soviet opposition; the USSR entered eastern Poland on September 17 under the secret protocol. Japan's government was reportedly shocked by the pact, and the fallout contributed to Tokyo seeking an armistice at Khalkhin Gol, concluded in mid-September 1939.
long_term_outcome: Over the following 22 months the USSR annexed the Baltic states and Bessarabia and fought the Winter War against Finland, broadly along the secret protocol's lines. On June 22, 1941, Germany broke the pact and invaded the Soviet Union, and Soviet forces suffered catastrophic early losses despite repeated intelligence warnings in the preceding months. The Soviet government denied the secret protocol's existence until 1989, when the USSR formally acknowledged it.
uncertainty_factors: Poland's transit veto held by a party not at the table
No enforcement on a German promise
Germany's invasion timetable not under Soviet control
An unresolved second front against Japan

options.label: Sign the non-aggression pact with Germany
options.short_description: Accept Ribbentrop's proposal for a bilateral German-Soviet non-aggression treaty with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence, and let the Triple Alliance talks lapse.
options.upside: Removes the immediate prospect of a two-front war while fighting is already underway against Japan in the east; pushes any future German attack further from Soviet core territory via the buffer in the secret protocol; buys time free of a German threat to keep rebuilding the Red Army; and keeps the USSR out of an immediate war over Poland that Britain and France, not the USSR, are committed to fight.
options.downside: Publicly aligns the Soviet Union with Nazi Germany, reversing the collective-security diplomacy the USSR had pursued since the mid-1930s; frees Hitler to attack Poland without fear of an immediate second front; and supplies Germany with trade and material at the outset of its war.
known_tradeoffs: The Triple Alliance talks have stalled on exactly the question Voroshilov called make-or-break, with neither Western delegation able to resolve it and neither Poland nor Romania showing any sign of conceding; the German offer is the only one of the two that can actually be concluded before Germany moves. versus It rests entirely on trusting a German promise with no external enforcement, and leaves open what happens once Germany's western campaigns end and it can turn east.

options.label: Keep pursuing the Triple Alliance with Britain and France
options.short_description: Persist with the Moscow military talks and keep pressing for a binding tripartite convention despite the transit-rights impasse and the limited authority of the Western delegations.
options.upside: Keeps the USSR aligned with the Western powers against further German expansion, preserves the anti-fascist posture of Soviet diplomacy, and -- if it produced a binding convention -- confronts Germany with a real prospect of a two-front war. It also keeps the USSR out of any part in the partition of Poland and the Baltic states.
options.downside: The talks have not moved past the single issue identified as decisive, and neither Poland nor Romania shows any sign of yielding; the British and French delegations cannot bind their governments beyond what they have already offered. Waiting carries no guarantee of resolution and no timetable, while Germany's own schedule for Poland is not under Soviet control.
known_tradeoffs: A genuine three-power alliance is a stronger deterrent in principle than a bilateral deal with the very power it is meant to contain. versus Continued delay as Germany's move on Poland approaches, with no assurance the transit impasse is ever resolved, risks leaving the USSR isolated against Germany in the west and Japan in the east with nothing concluded on either side.

case_information.content: British and French military delegations arrived in Moscow on August 11, 1939 for the Triple Alliance talks, sent by slow merchant ship (the City of Exeter) rather than by air or fast warship. The British delegation, headed by Admiral Reginald Drax, had no written authority to conclude a binding military convention.

On August 14, 1939, Voroshilov asked the British and French delegations directly whether Poland and Romania would permit Soviet troops to cross their territory to engage German forces. Neither delegation could answer for Poland, and Poland's government under Foreign Minister Jozef Beck continued to refuse consent, fearing that Soviet forces once admitted would not leave.

Voroshilov told the British and French delegations that without a positive answer on transit, 'all the efforts to enter into a military convention are doomed to failure' -- a position the Soviet side held through the last military-committee session on August 21, after which the talks were suspended indefinitely.

Since May 1939 Soviet forces had been fighting a large undeclared border war against Japan at Khalkhin Gol on the Mongolian-Manchurian frontier, involving more than 100,000 troops on both sides. The decisive Soviet offensive under Zhukov began on August 20, 1939, while both the Moscow talks and the German approach were still live.

Germany's offer, pressed with increasing urgency through August, combined a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol assigning Finland, Estonia, Latvia, eastern Poland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere of influence.

On August 19, 1939, Germany and the USSR signed a commercial credit agreement giving the Soviet Union a 200-million-Reichsmark line of credit for German industrial goods, presented by German officials as the first step in reshaping the political relationship.

Soviet officials read the slow travel, junior rank and missing full powers of the British and French delegations as evidence that London and Paris were not treating the military talks with urgency. This was the Soviet reading at the time; whether it was the correct explanation is disputed.

Germany would invade Poland on September 1, 1939, just over a week after the pact was signed. Some German attack on Poland was anticipated in general terms, but the precise date was not knowable at the decision point.
Germany would break the pact and invade the Soviet Union on June 22, 1941 -- something that could not be known with any certainty in August 1939, nearly two years earlier.

When the invasion came in 1941, Soviet forces would be caught largely unprepared despite numerous intelligence warnings in the preceding months. That failure of threat assessment, centred on Stalin personally, was not foreordained by the 1939 pact and could not have been anticipated at the decision point.

Whether a genuinely concluded Triple Alliance -- had the transit objection somehow been resolved -- would have deterred Hitler from invading Poland at all, brought on a broader war on terms less favourable to Germany, or simply drawn the USSR into war in September 1939 on the Western powers' timetable, is unknowable and remains contested among historians.

evidence.title: The Alliance That Failed: Moscow and the Triple Alliance Negotiations, 1939
evidence.citation: Roberts, G. (1996). 'The Alliance That Failed: Moscow and the Triple Alliance Negotiations, 1939.' European History Quarterly, 26(3).
evidence.supported_claim: The course and breakdown of the Anglo-Franco-Soviet military talks: the delegations' composition and authority, Voroshilov's August 14 question on transit rights, and the impasse that suspended the talks after August 21.

evidence.title: The Soviet Union and the Origins of the Second World War: Russo-German Relations and the Road to War, 1933-1941
evidence.citation: Roberts, G. (1995). The Soviet Union and the Origins of the Second World War. Macmillan.
evidence.supported_claim: The interpretation of the pact as a defensive, buffer-seeking Soviet response to failed Western talks -- one position in a live historiographical dispute, not a settled reading.

evidence.title: Telegram from Ambassador Laurence A. Steinhardt to the Secretary of State, August 23, 1939
evidence.author_or_institution: United States Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1939, Volume I
evidence.supported_claim: A contemporary diplomatic report, dated the day the pact was signed, that Poland's continued refusal made an Anglo-Franco-Soviet agreement impossible and that a late Polish reversal would likely come too late.

evidence.title: Secret Additional Protocol to the Treaty of Nonaggression Between Germany and the U.S.S.R.
evidence.author_or_institution: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School (hosting the German Foreign Office / Nuremberg document text)
evidence.supported_claim: The text of the secret protocol and the spheres of influence it assigned -- Finland, Estonia, Latvia, eastern Poland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere.

evidence.title: Memorandum by Karl Schnurre on the German-Soviet Credit Agreement of August 19, 1939
evidence.author_or_institution: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School (German Foreign Office document)
evidence.publication_date: Memorandum dated August 29, 1939, describing the August 19, 1939 agreement
evidence.supported_claim: The August 19 commercial credit agreement, its 200-million-Reichsmark line of credit, and how German officials framed it as the first step toward a political realignment.

evidence.supported_claim: The scale and timing of the undeclared Soviet-Japanese war at Khalkhin Gol, Zhukov's August 20 offensive, and the pact's effect on Japanese policy and the September armistice.

evidence.title: The Forgotten Soviet-Japanese War of 1939
evidence.supported_claim: Accessible summary of the same author's research on Khalkhin Gol as a live second front during the August 1939 decision.

evidence.title: Source disagreements recorded in the research record
evidence.author_or_institution: Research record for this case (see src-01 through src-10)
evidence.supported_claim: Two points remain contested. First, how far the pact enabled the invasion of Poland: some historians, Roberts among them, read it as a defensive Soviet response and hold that Hitler's timetable was already set, while others treat it as the decisive factor removing Germany's two-front risk. The record supports that Hitler wanted the pact specifically to neutralise the Soviet factor; how much the September 1 timing depended on it is not resolved. Second, how seriously Britain and France pursued the talks: the junior delegations, the slow sea voyage and the missing full powers support a reading of half-heartedness, but others argue London and Paris faced real constraints -- reluctance to alarm Poland, disbelief that Stalin would deal with Hitler -- and that the failure was mutual mistrust rather than one-sided bad faith.
